Caravancol's Classic Is a Proper Vintage-Inspired Travel Trailer That Fits As Many as Six People
6 photos
Photo: Caravancol
There are so many different brands in the world spitting out what they feel is the perfect vintage teardrop camper that we can easily get lost in all the details. However, every once in a while, a particular team comes along and shows us how it’s done. That crew is Caravancol, a Spain-born manufacturer banking on vintage design to grab everyone’s attention.
When I first saw the Classic from Caravancol, I couldn’t but help be reminded of American campers from back in the day, and I know that it’s the side panels at the kitchen that give us this impression . But what we’re working with here is actually a very modern camper, one built with timeless and trusted materials to give off that retro look.
Photo: Caravancol Materials like aluminum, wood, and composite insulation are called upon to give rise to the modern but retro Classic. It has an aluminum exterior that’s coated to keep the elements at bay, bamboo interior paneling, foam core insulation, and a plywood kitchen that looks downright flawless.
One neat trait is that the sides of the Classic are reinforced. We don’t know how, but they are, and it’s the main reason why we can see them carrying roof-top racks. So, these babies are clearly not so traditional in the sense that they do call upon modern building methods to give rise to it. Personally, I don’t know of a whole lot of traditional teardrop campers that can handle the added weight of a tent and occupants on its roof.
How much are we talking here? According to the spec sheet, up to 750 kg (1,653 lbs) is the max that a Classic can handle, and there’s a reason for that: it’s built over in Europe. Out there, you can operate an unbraked travel trailer as long as its GVWR remains at 750 kg or less and the combined weight of the trailer and vehicle doesn’t exceed 3,500 kg, without any special driver’s license classes.
Photo: Caravancol In its lightest configuration, the Classic also weighs a meaningless and very manageable weight of just 550 kg (1,213 lbs).
That however, sems to be the standard layout, with the manufacturer’s website showcasing additional upgrades, some of which do mess with the running gear and unlock brakes and axles with shock absorbers. Sounds like this one can handle some off-road use.
Speaking of upgrades, do note that the roof-rack is an optional feature here and will cost you a bit more to include in your build. If you do, however, it unlocks family use. Keep in mind that Caravancol mentions that sleeping capacity in their campers can be extended to as many as six.
While most of us are sure to think that this is made possible with an additional annex – it can – from what I could make out, the interior of a Classic can also include a bunk system for kids. If the tent is a three-person one, which the market does offer, then that’s that, six people. It’s not often that we can tap into this sort of ability with a teardrop camper.
Photo: Caravancol Before heading inside, allow me to point out that the exterior of this unit can also handle countless other pieces of gear, including a shower, solar panels, AC and heating units, and even a skylight. The latter does replace the AC, but falling asleep while staring at the stars is a must.
Oh, and let’s not forget the gorgeous and inspiring kitchen block, located at the rear of the camper, in traditional fashion. We have access to a cooker here, fridge, sink with water, ample cabinetry, and the electrical systems necessary to power said fridge and even coffee makers, kettles, all of that jazz.
Again, those side skirts also give this one its unique and vintage touch and is a feature that is used across the entire lineup from Caravancol. Couple that with the stained wood look, and you can see why I call this one vintage.
Photo: Caravancol The interior has that whole classic look and feel to it too, again, brought to life with the use of wood, in this case, mostly bamboo, and the cabinetry at the foot of the bed. Keep in mind that we can also call upon a TV and antenna and a modular mattress too, the latter being essential for adding a lounge experience inside.
A couple things to consider here are clearly price and the fact that this one is European, marking it as hand-off for anyone outside of that continent. You’ll have to handle shipping and DOT clearance if you do ship one outside of Europe.
As for the amount of cash that we need to drop on this one, Caravancol showcases a price tag of €16,800 ($18,800), and that seems to be without sales tax or VAT, as it’s called over in Europe. That said, there are some custom camper shops in the US that can spit out a camper like this one, so it may be best to act locally. Enjoy the trips out there.
